title: The great idler
hook: a teaching book tells its reader that all the reading won't settle them until they forget it all
carry: drop the doer, not the work

segments.voice: Yesterday, shukti and the sage's test: why does the king still reach for silver that's only a shell? Wanting grows from forgetting the self.
screen: `THE ASHTAVAKRA GITA.` · `WANTING GROWS FROM FORGETTING THE SELF.`

segments.voice: Somewhere on a shelf there's a stack of books about letting go, and every one of them is something else to hold on to. The Ashtavakra Gita seems to know that joke. Deep in the book, the sage says something that could make a diligent reader put the page down. You can talk about the scriptures and listen to them, my child, as much as you like. But you won't rest in yourself until you forget it all. A book telling its reader that the reading isn't the point. And a few verses later, it praises a master of idleness.
screen: `BOOKS ABOUT LETTING GO.` → `FORGET IT ALL.` → `A MASTER OF IDLENESS.`

segments.voice: This is chapter sixteen, in paraphrase. After the line about forgetting, the sage goes on. You may enjoy, you may work, you may meditate, but the mind will still long for what lies beyond all that, where wanting goes quiet. Then something like a diagnosis: everyone is unhappy because of their striving, and nobody notices. Then a verse that can sound like a joke. Happy is the great idler, the one for whom even opening and closing the eyes is a bother. Read straight, that's a blessing on the couch. Many teachers read it another way, because the verses around it are about one kind of effort: the strain of the one who thinks, I am the doer. The Bhagavad Gita names that strain plainly. Deluded by ahamkara, the ego, a person thinks, I am the doer. And the one who knows the truth, it says, thinks, while seeing, hearing, walking, even breathing, I do nothing at all. That's one of Hinduism's big teachings: the work goes on, and the ego's claim on it drops. So the great idler isn't someone who won't wash the dishes. The dishes still get washed; nobody inside is clenching about it. The forgetting is read the same way. The sage isn't asking Janaka to forget his kindness or his duties. He's asking him to stop holding the teaching like a possession, one more thing for the ego to own. The book has pointed at freedom for pages; now even the pointing drops away.
screen: `FORGET IT ALL.` · `UNHAPPY BECAUSE OF STRIVING.` · `AHAMKARA: 'I AM THE DOER.'` · `'I DO NOTHING AT ALL,' WHILE THE WORK GOES ON.` · then, large: `DROP THE DOER, NOT THE WORK.`

segments.voice: For these minutes, try the sage's kind of idleness: don't manage the breath, don't follow a technique, don't try to remember anything. Let breathing, hearing and seeing happen, and notice they happen without anyone pushing them. If you catch yourself trying to sit well, let that go too. If you pray, close the way many Hindus close an action, offering it: Krishnarpanam, given to Krishna.
Great idler, the one in whom the inner striving has stopped, because the ego's I am the doer has gone quiet. Today, the Ashtavakra Gita's hardest line: forget it all.
Your line: drop the doer, not the work. The dishes still get washed. Same time tomorrow.

howItsDone: Some teachers of the Ashtavakra Gita read its praise of idleness, with Bhagavad Gita 3.27 and 5.8, as the end of the ego's sense of being the doer rather than of outward work; some Hindus close an action or a puja by offering it, with words like Sri Krishnarpanamastu.

fork.reveal: chapter sixteen says it plainly: talk and listen as much as you like, but rest comes only when you forget it all.

trapdoor: what you thought: the great idler is a blessing on doing nothing.
what it means: the straining that stops is the ego's I am the doer; the work, and the teaching's purpose, go on.

chat.meaning: The great idler in chapter sixteen is the one whose ego has stopped claiming, I am the doer. The Gita's knower still acts, and thinks, I do nothing at all.
